title: Bridging the gap: Evaluating the divide between legal obligations, policy and practice in adult prison education in England
abstract: Abstract With legal rights to prison education for adults well-established under domestic and international standards, this narrative review explores the historical and contemporary policy frameworks and legal obligations guiding provision in public prisons in England. Addressing an international readership of practitioners, academics and policymakers, it scrutinises the implementation and delivery of prison education following years of government and parliamentary reviews reporting poor outcomes. It draws on publicly available documents to identify key issues, including chronic under-resourcing, insufficient digital infrastructure, inadequate systems for identifying and monitoring learning needs, poor basic skills outcomes and insufficient support for prisoners with additional educational needs and learning disabilities. The analysis reveals persistent access inequalities compared to community further education, deficits in legal entitlements and systemic challenges faced by education providers and prison governors. title: Transformative learning as a reflection of social innovation education: A theoretical-empirical framework
abstract: Abstract The literature suggests that social innovation in education can generate transformative learning. This article examines the curriculum and practices of a Brazilian school, building upon the framework proposed by the authors in 2023. A case study, documentary research, non-participant observation and semi-structured interviews were conducted and thematically analysed using content analysis. The results demonstrate a model of education that fosters autonomy and contributes to participants’ emancipation. Inspired by the work of Paulo Freire, this qualitative exploratory study concludes by suggesting future studies, such as a contextual comparative analysis of the resistance of actors involved in innovation. It provides insights to improve practices and develop new models of educational management, putting forward a vision of education that is autonomous and contributes to the emancipation of those involved in citizenship and social roles. This benefits both management and education researchers, as well as the actors within the educational system itself.

title: Unlocking undergraduate access to higher education: Recognition of prior learning in South Africa
abstract: Abstract This research note presents the University of the Western Cape’s Portfolio Development Hybrid Programme (PDHP) as a nationally recognised, pedagogically grounded model of recognition of prior learning (RPL) for undergraduate access in South Africa. Designed to enable adult learners – many without formal qualifications or with marginalised knowledge backgrounds – to enter and succeed in higher education, PDHP combines values-based curriculum design with transformative pedagogies rooted in adult learning, epistemic justice and care. Drawing on five years of longitudinal data (2020–2024) and more than two decades of institutional implementation, the study illustrates how RPL can evolve from a once-off assessment mechanism into a sustained teaching-and-learning intervention that builds academic readiness and social mobility within the adult learning context. title: Cultivating critical global citizenship education through defamiliarisation and collaborative online international learning
abstract: Abstract This study employed Norman Fairclough’s three-dimensional approach to critical discourse analysis to investigate the potential of defamiliarisation, supported by collaborative online international learning, to help pre-service teachers in South Africa and Germany challenge neoliberalism and promote critical global citizenship. A group of pre-service teachers in South Africa and Germany ( N = 54) were prompted to critically analyse capitalism’s global influence and articulate their ideas using creative illustrations inspired by the short online film Marx and I . The resulting artwork of a sub-sample of the South African student teachers ( n = 7) shows their individual and collective reflections on global injustice, capitalism and human rights abuses, while that of the German student teachers ( n = 7) emphasises the refugee crisis in Europe, environmental degradation and social exclusion. The research highlights the usefulness of defamiliarisation in producing context-specific criticisms and transforming student teachers’ perceptions of global socio-political environments. title: Teacher professionalisation at the intersection of open, moral and critical Global Citizenship Education: Reflections from an international comparative study
abstract: Abstract New social contracts for education, such as those promoted by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and the Dublin Declaration on Global Education to 2050, outline the need to prepare student teachers to be change agents who can help address growing global challenges, using innovative Global Citizenship Education (GCE) approaches. To create and offer their students experimental learning opportunities on how to deal with these challenges, student teachers need to develop global sensitivity and position themselves to think globally, act locally and reflect “glocally”. While various models have been developed to describe these competencies in teacher education, research about their effectiveness is still emerging. The study presented in this article outlines the formal evaluation of an Erasmus+ project on developing global sensitivity in 301 student teachers (187 female, 114 male) from five partner universities. The project developed an interculturally sensitive teacher training concept designed to facilitate an international virtual exchange between the student teachers. title: Enriching a critical emancipatory approach to global citizenship education: Conceptual reflections on using Oskar Negt’s “creation of context” as leitmotif
abstract: Abstract This conceptual article aims to enrich critical emancipatory perspectives on global citizenship education by drawing upon the meta-competence “creation of context” introduced by German social philosopher and adult educator Oskar Negt (1934–2024). Negt is well-known in Germany (though not so much elsewhere) for his landmark work on critical theory (in the context of the so-called “Frankfurt School”), social sciences and (adult) education. The authors of this article discuss his seminal perspective with reference to two other theoretical approaches that are also widely discussed in Germany but have yet to enter the debate in education and social sciences elsewhere. First, they address the critical theory on education and liberation proposed by Heinz-Joachim Heydorn in his paper on the contradiction between education ( Bildung ) and domination. Second, they elaborate on the social diagnosis of the imperial mode of living proposed by Ulrich Brand and Markus Wissen, which features in contemporary discourse on the emancipatory power and potential of education in Germany. title: Global citizenship education within virtual global engagement: Ethical challenges and possibilities
abstract: Abstract This case study considers the ethical challenges faced by programme developers leading a virtual engagement programme aimed at developing global citizenship that reaches from the university to communities around the world. The programme is IGlobal, which was launched by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign’s College of Education during the COVID-19 pandemic as a virtual replacement for teach abroad programming. It is a virtual global engagement project that links participants from over 20 countries spanning the Global North and Global South. Applying the framework for ethical global citizenship education (EGCE) proposed by Emiliano Bosio and Hans Schattle, this qualitative study used interviews, focus group discussions, document analysis and programme observation to consider the ways in which the framework can guide practice and illuminate particular challenges in global community engagement, as well as the areas that the framework may not reach. Since the focus was on the programme developers’ experience, the pupils being taught through the IGlobal programme were not themselves surveyed for this case study. title: Reimagining global citizenship education: Decolonial dialogues across Australia, Colombia and Mexico
abstract: Abstract This article presents a comparative analysis of global citizenship education (GCE) in three national contexts: Australia, Colombia and Mexico. The systematic examination of these contexts contributes to understanding GCE through a critical and decolonial lens. The comparative study analyses national education policy discourse as a starting point for systematising experiences. It engages in an epistemic dialogue between the Global South (specifically Latin America/Abya Yala), represented by Colombia and Mexico, and the Global North, represented by Australia. Despite Australias predominantly Global North-oriented education policy, the study also examines student mobilisations and discusses issues such as Indigenous rights and planetary responsibility. These dialogues open avenues for alternative visions, rooted in critical interculturality and planetary care. Methodologically, the study draws on Stephen Balls heuristic approach to analyse education policy through a poststructuralist sociological lens, considering policy context and the influence of policy as discourse. title: Global citizenship education in a post-disaster context in Aceh, Indonesia: perspectives of student teachers
abstract: Abstract This article examines how student teachers in a post-disaster context make sense of global citizenship education (GCE) through a combination of Pancasila (an Indigenous philosophy derived from Sanskrit) and citizenship education (together referred to as PPKn) in Aceh Province, Indonesia. This qualitative study involved a group of final-year student teachers (6 male and 2 female) who were undertaking teaching practice as part of their teacher education programme in 2020. Based on semi-structured interview data, the findings suggest that participants engaged with GCE in various ways – through formal education, everyday encounters and historical narratives of armed conflict and the tsunami disaster. The authors argue that approaching GCE through a local–global prism provides a nuanced understanding and exposes tensions between the predominantly secular orientation of GCE in the Global North and the Islamic orientation of PPKn in Aceh Province. Their findings highlight how student teachers make sense of the values and beliefs they develop through PPKn and how these resonate with or diverge from normative GCE values. title: Teacher agency for Indigenous languages in education: A decolonial perspective from Nepal
abstract: Abstract This article explores the role of teacher agency for Indigenous language education through a decolonial lens. Dominant views and practices of educational development and language policy often exclude teachers as mere implementers of top-down policy. Yet there is growing recognition of their crucial role in shaping policy at the micro level. Drawing on the example of four male teachers from Nepal, the authors examine how teachers develop and use their agency to create spaces for Indigenous languages. Building on a critical and decolonial perspective, the authors conceptualise teacher agency in language policy as a collective, political and relational phenomenon which extends well beyond the classroom. Their approach emphasises community connection and accountability, calling into question individual-centric frameworks. They conclude by calling for critical dialogue with Indigenous language teachers and a decolonial re-evaluation of teacher agency that respects Indigenous knowledge systems as a prerequisite for linguistically sustaining education.

title: Sustainability-related learning in adulthood: Exploring the topics and characteristics of adults involved in sustainability-related learning activities
abstract: Abstract This article focuses on adults’ informal learning related to sustainability, addressing a central gap in adult education research through a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods. Drawing on data from the German National Educational Panel Study (NEPS), the authors investigate which sustainability-related learning topics adults mention in open-ended responses and in which learning contexts these topics emerge. They analyse open-ended responses of adults aged 35–75 ( N = 6,793) across four survey waves (2017–2022), covering informal learning in different contexts (trade fairs and conferences, specialist lectures, digital learning programmes and internet-based learning opportunities). Based on these responses, they developed a deductive–inductive category system that served as the basis for coding a total of 17,395 statements. Building on this, they explore the characteristics, such as sociodemographics, personality traits and generalised values, of individuals who engage intensively with ecological sustainability topics across different contexts and over time. title: Exploring the potential of the Prakerja digital training programme as a social justice strategy for women entrepreneurs in Indonesia
abstract: Abstract Despite the increase in Indonesian women entrepreneurs, persistent gender inequality is evident in the lower sales and profits generated by women-owned enterprises compared to those owned by men. Although not specifically tailored to women, one governmental initiative, Kartu Prakerja [literally “pre-employment card”], aimed to increase access to training and enhance entrepreneurial skills. Launched in April 2020, this digital training programme was a strategic effort to address gender inequality in business ownership in Indonesia. The article explores the social justice potential of Prakerja to assist women entrepreneurs by providing redistributive justice, recognitive justice and representational justice : the three dimensions of social justice identified by Nancy Fraser. The study applied a multi-stage critical document analysis to materials published between 2020 and 2024. While the authors found that Prakerja could be considered a social justice strategy for women entrepreneurs, their analysis also suggests that the outcomes could have been further improved through consideration of intentional design across all three social justice dimensions. title: To be (or not to be) a global citizen in an algorithmic world? A cartographic, ethical and reflexive framework for higher education
abstract: Abstract As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reshapes educational priorities, governance and pedagogical norms, global citizenship education (GCE) in higher education (HE) faces intensifying tensions between ethical imperatives and algorithmic rationalities. This article offers a human-centred, critical-decolonial reframing of GCE in the era of artificial intelligence (AI). It argues that the dominant approaches to GCE risk reinforcing neoliberal, technocratic and universalist assumptions. Drawing on the work of Vanessa Andreotti, Sharon Stein, Emiliano Bosio and Paulo Freire, the article advocates for an alternative grounded in relational ethics, epistemic plurality and institutional reflexivity. Employing critical interpretive synthesis and guided by the performative tool of social cartography , the authors developed a ten-dimension framework for institutional self-reflection. Rather than framing GCE as a fixed set of global competencies, this framework reimagines it as a dynamic pedagogical project grounded in care, shared responsibility and ethical dialogue. title: Global citizenship education overlooked: Curriculum policies and progressive nationalism
abstract: Abstract Over the last few years, left-wing governments in anglophone countries, from the United States to Aotearoa New Zealand, have increasingly embraced what could be termed progressive nationalism . This political project rhetorically combines progressive ideals, such as inclusion, identity politics and wellbeing, with the exaltation of a national identity. Perhaps shadowed by the global emergence of national/authoritarian populisms, this phenomenon has gone largely unnoticed by global citizenship scholars. In this article, the author first develops the concept of progressive nationalism in New Zealand. After considering the historical context and revisiting the role of school curricula in the spread of globalist/nationalist ideologies, the article explores the imprint of progressive nationalism in the recent curriculum policies of New Zealand’s former Labour Government (2017–2023). The historical and ideological analysis of the “curriculum struggles” associated with these policies reveals a clear move towards the local/national at the expense of the global. title: Between superdiversity and doing diversity: School-based parent cafés as places of parent education
abstract: Abstract Critics often point out that parental education programmes primarily reach (formally) educated middle-class parents. Even in superdiverse urban neighbourhoods in Germany, schools struggle to cater to parents on the lower end of the socioeconomic spectrum. This qualitative study showcases school-based parent cafés in Hamburg, aiming to find out how their agenda and implementation correspond regarding the anticipated superdiversity of the target groups and the perceived diversity of the participants. The author draws on a concept triad of “superdiversity”, “diversity” and “doing diversity” to illustrate how socio-spatial developments and the resulting superdiversity among parents (macro level) are taken up in schools (meso level) and realised at the micro level in the sense of doing diversity. The study’s main finding is that while the composition of café participants is diverse, it is not yet representative enough to reflect the superdiversity of parents in schools’ catchment areas. title: Understanding Europe’s skills shortage: Patterns of participation in formal and non-formal education and training
abstract: Abstract Technological advancements, environmental commitments and demographic shifts are rapidly reshaping Europe’s labour markets, and thus the skills needed to succeed within them. These changes are driving growth in some industries while leading to contractions in others. Adult learning, both in formal and non-formal contexts, provides pathways for reskilling and upskilling, which are critical for adapting to these shifts. Recognising the importance of education and training, the European Union (EU) set a target that, by 2025, at least 47 per cent of adults aged 24–64 should have participated in some form of learning, education or training during the last 12 months. Using data from the EU Labour Force Survey (EU-LFS), which ran from 2013 to 2022, this article explores progress towards that target, specifically examining the relationship between personal and work-related factors and participation in different forms of learning. The results show that participation in adult education and training has grown significantly, particularly in job-related, non-formal training. journal_name: International Review of Education / Internationale Zeitschrift für Erziehungswissenschaft
title: MOOCs and universities for sustainable development: A fading nexus?
abstract: Abstract The quality of, and access to, education for sustainable development (ESD) are at the forefront of e-learning. Assuming that there are opportunities to judiciously examine the potential of massive open online courses (MOOCs) to foster ESD, this article carries out a multi-method scoping review to identify emerging research themes and analyse gaps in the literature, based on: (1) an environmental scan of sustainable development-related MOOCs; (2) a rapid bibliometric analysis (RBA) of literature on the nexus between MOOCs, universities and sustainable development; and (3) a case study of a MOOC entitled “Globalisation and Sustainable Development”. The main contribution of this article to the field is to demonstrate the scale of sustainable development-related MOOCs, the marginal impact of universities in fostering the 2030 Agenda through MOOCs, and the challenges faced by university administrations in utilising MOOCs as a vehicle to advance ESD during a period of financial uncertainty. Based on these findings, the article discusses the potential and pitfalls of MOOCs in fostering ESD in the post-pandemic world.

title: An escape game in a museum as an opportunity to enhance visitors’ environmental attitudes
abstract: Abstract Museums are places for informal education. The Observatory and Science Experience Centre in Eger, Hungary, has been using different entertaining methods for this purpose for some time. Recently, however, curators identified the need for a new game to enhance visitors’ environmental attitudes and awareness. They decided to address this issue using an escape game. This game type has the advantage of being a popular form of entertainment for both younger and older people, and even for whole families – a good fit for the Observatory’s visitor structure. Research has shown that escape games lead to a promising, albeit statistically not significant increase in players’ environmental attitude scores. In light of these considerations, the aim of the study presented here was to examine whether the escape game designed for the Observatory’s purposes would be effective in improving visitors’ environmental attitudes. To answer this question, the author used the environmental emotion sub-scale (EESS) from the “Environmental Attitude” questionnaire developed in 2019 by Naim Uzun, Kenneth L. title: Balancing the books: Understanding the motivations and challenges of part-time students as lifelong learners and “resilient negotiators”
abstract: Abstract This study examines the motivations and challenges faced by adult learners engaged in part-time study as a form of lifelong learning. It focuses on how they balance competing demands from work, family and study. Applying a theoretical framework of self-directed learning (SDL) and adult learning theory (ALT), the author interviewed 25 part-time students (7 female, 18 male) based in Southeast Asia, all of whom were employed or self-employed. The study identified three core motivations (namely, support systems, personal development and career growth) and three major challenges (namely, balancing responsibilities, time management, and the need for resilience and adaptability). The concept of the “resilient negotiator” emerged as a central theoretical contribution. This idea represents how learners strategically manage limited resources such as time or money, and the expectations of others. The findings of this study have practical implications for universities, employers and policymakers in supporting lifelong learners through the provision of flexible delivery models, supportive policies and institutional incentives. title: To enrol or not to enrol: What are the risks in choosing a massive open online course (MOOC)?
abstract: Abstract Massive open online courses (MOOCs) offer a unique opportunity for lifelong learning by providing a learning platform for a large and diverse audience. Although their popularity is still growing, industry experts had anticipated a higher level of acceptance than has actually occurred. One possible reason for the slower-than-expected growth is the perceived risk to learners. This study examines the factors influencing MOOC adoption based on perceived risk theory. Using survey-based quantitative analysis (with responses from 300 university students), the authors define four main dimensions of perceived risk: value, non-financial investment, social risk and security. Their findings show that uncertainty about the value offered by MOOCs is one of the most important dimensions in assessing risk. The second most important risk factor is learners’ non-financial investment. The main sources of this investment, time and effort, are finite for learners and thus represent a critical dimension in the educational context of risk research. journal_name: International Review of Education / Internationale Zeitschrift für Erziehungswissenschaft
title: The effects of volunteering on individual growth, professional development and community life: The case of the Movimento Transformers Youth Association, Portugal
abstract: Abstract This study focuses on the impact of the Movimento Transformers Youth Association on individual growth, professional development and community life. It explores how the organisation, through its “SuperPower schools” methodology, empowers Portuguese youth, fostering talent for social good. Using a qualitative approach including interviews and focus group discussions, the study captures the nuances of the volunteering programme’s influence across different stakeholder groups, sustained by the multifaceted nature of volunteering. The Movimento Transformers programme exemplifies how structured volunteering can encourage individual and societal progress, enhancing individual growth, professional development and community engagement. The study is limited by its singular focus on one organisation, suggesting a need for further comparative research to substantiate the findings across similar programmes. Nevertheless, this research underscores the value of structured volunteering programmes in youth development, with implications for policymakers and educators aiming to replicate effective engagement models.
